items.passage:
These smart cities will be the cities of the future. They will use (1) __________ technologies to improve their infrastructure and services. 
 Infrastructure will become more (2) __________ and eco-friendly. This will be achieved by reducing the use of natural resources and the amount of waste. In addition, city dwellers will have access to a transport system that combines different modes of transport such as buses, underground and overground trains, and is (3) __________ and easy to use. Smart cities will also have larger pedestrian zones and more cycle paths. Poor areas will be rebuilt to make all neighbourhoods safer and cleaner. This will provide better living spaces for the growing population and improve people’s (4) __________ of living. 
 Most services will be offered online, and will be (5) __________ for everybody to use. People will also be able to give and receive feedback, monitor programmes and activities with the help of virtual tours of worksites. In addition, many health and education services will be (6) __________ online, ensuring a pleasant experience for residents. (7) __________, people will be able to book an appointment to see a doctor online. They will also receive prescriptions and all the necessary documents at home. Improved infrastructure and efficient services will make the cities of the future more (8) __________ and will provide a better quality of life to city dwellers.

items.stem:
Where in the passage does the following sentence best fit? 
 The risk begins when convenience becomes the city’s favourite excuse.
items.passage:
At the corner, a sensor changes the traffic light before the junction clogs. A phone warns that the air near the main road is poor, so cyclists take a quieter route. None of this feels dramatic. That is the point. The future city enters daily life not as a shining exhibition, but as small acts of friction removed . 
 [I]  The smarter version of a city is not simply one covered with cameras, apps, and computer-controlled systems. Its real promise lies in connecting scattered services so that public transport runs smoothly, energy is used efficiently, and residents have access to safer facilities without navigating a maze of offices. Used well, data can reveal where traffic flow breaks down, where emissions rise, and where a neighbourhood lacks green space. Not only can technology speed up decision making, it can also make old urban neglect harder to hide. 
 [II] A security camera may protect a pedestrian zone, but it may also teach people to accept constant monitoring as the price of feeling safe. [III] Predictive tools can help officials plan bus routes, while the same tools, built on poor or partial data, may overlook isolated residents, informal workers, or suburbs with weak digital access. Awareness asks what people need and gives them clearer choices . Exploitation sells their fear of crime, pollution, or falling behind, then calls the sale innovation. 
 [IV] A liveable city, then, is not the one with the most impressive technology. It is the one whose systems remain answerable to residents, including those who do not speak the language of platforms and dashboards. Rarely is the deepest problem the sensor itself. The harder question is who installs it, who reads its signals, who benefits from the prediction, and who disappears inside the average. If smart design cannot make room for trust, privacy, and a sense of community, the city may become efficient in a strangely lonely way.
